title: BST: insert & search

hook.scenario: Searching an unsorted list takes O(n) time. Binary search on a sorted array takes O(log n), but inserting a new element takes O(n) shift time. How can we get O(log n) search AND O(log n) insertion?
hook.question: How does a tree structure allow both searching and inserting in log-n time?

why_it_exists.problem: Sorted arrays allow O(log n) search via binary search, but inserting a new item requires O(n) array element shifting. Unsorted lists allow fast insertion but slow O(n) searches.
why_it_exists.naive_solution: Using sorted arrays for lookup and re-sorting or shifting array entries on every insert.
why_it_exists.better_idea: Use a Binary Search Tree (BST) where left subtree < node < right subtree. Descending the tree halves the search space at each step, achieving O(log n) lookup and dynamic O(log n) pointer-based insertion.

mental_model.intuition: Binary search turned into a dynamic pointer tree structure.
mental_model.description: At each node, compare the target key to `node.val`. If target is smaller, move to `node.left` (discarding the entire right subtree). If larger, move to `node.right` (discarding the entire left subtree). For insertion, follow this search path until reaching a null child reference, then attach the new node there.
mental_model.repeated_decision: target vs this node -- go LEFT (smaller) or RIGHT (larger)?

explanation:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree that satisfies the strict BST Ordering Invariant at EVERY node:
- All keys in `node.left` subtree are strictly LESS than `node.val`.
- All keys in `node.right` subtree are strictly GREATER than `node.val`.

Searching in a BST:
1. If `node is None`, target is not present (return None).
2. If `target == node.val`, target found (return node).
3. If `target < node.val`, recurse `search(node.left, target)`.
4. If `target > node.val`, recurse `search(node.right, target)`.

Inserting in a BST:
To insert key `val`:
1. Follow the search path for `val`.
2. When you reach a `None` child slot, create `TreeNode(val)` and attach it to the parent.
3. Insertion always lands at a new leaf node at a unique deterministic spot.

Walkthrough on BST Search and Insert:
Given BST:
       8
      / \
     3   10
    / \
   1   6

Search for target `6`:
- Compare 6 vs 8: 6 < 8 -> go left to 3.
- Compare 6 vs 3: 6 > 3 -> go right to 6.
- Compare 6 vs 6: 6 == 6 -> Found!

Insert target `7`:
- Compare 7 vs 8 -> go left to 3.
- Compare 7 vs 3 -> go right to 6.
- Compare 7 vs 6 -> go right to 6.right (which is None).
- Attach `TreeNode(7)` as 6.right.

The Critical Degradation Caveat (Spindly Tree Trap):
If elements are inserted in already sorted order (e.g. `1, 2, 3, 4, 5`), the BST degrades into a single long line (a linked list). In this worst case, tree height `h = n`, and search/insert cost degrades from `O(log n)` to `O(n)`. Self-balancing BSTs (AVL, Red-Black trees) fix this by rebalancing during insertions.

key_points.title: BST Invariant
key_points.detail: For every node: max(left subtree) < node.val < min(right subtree).

key_points.title: Time Complexity
key_points.detail: O(h) for search and insert, where h is tree height. O(log n) when balanced; O(n) worst-case when skewed.

key_points.title: Unique Insertion Spot
key_points.detail: Every key has exactly one valid null slot where it can be inserted as a leaf while preserving the BST property.

common_mistakes.title: Assuming BST operations are ALWAYS O(log n)
common_mistakes.explanation: Standard BSTs have no self-balancing mechanism. Unbalanced insertion of sorted data creates a spindly tree with O(n) performance.

common_mistakes.title: Thinking insertion can reorder existing nodes
common_mistakes.explanation: Standard BST insertion never shifts or modifies existing tree nodes; it simply attaches a new leaf at the unique empty child slot.

common_mistakes.title: Unclear duplicate handling
common_mistakes.explanation: Failing to define how duplicates are handled. Standard practice either rejects duplicates or consistently routes them to the right subtree.

when_not_to_use.scenario: Data is already fully static and index lookups are constant
when_not_to_use.reason: Use a sorted array with binary search if no insertions take place (better cache locality).

when_not_to_use.scenario: O(1) average lookup is needed without range queries
when_not_to_use.reason: Use a Hash Map for O(1) key lookups if ordering and min/max/range queries are not needed.

failure_signals: You need dynamic insertions/deletions while maintaining sorted order.
You need to quickly query minimum, maximum, predecessor, or successor elements.

engineering_examples.title: C++ `std::set` / Java `TreeMap`
engineering_examples.problem: Maintain a dynamically changing collection of unique items in sorted order with range query support.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Under the hood, `std::set` and `TreeMap` use self-balancing BSTs (Red-Black trees) to guarantee O(log n) insert, search, and delete.

engineering_examples.title: Database B-Tree Indexes
engineering_examples.problem: Perform fast disk lookups and range scans on database column keys.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: B-Trees are multi-way generalizations of BSTs optimized for block storage, keeping search and insert logarithmic.

recall_questions.q: What is the core ordering invariant of a Binary Search Tree?
recall_questions.answer: For every node, all left subtree values are strictly less than node.val, and all right subtree values are strictly greater than node.val.

recall_questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching a non-balancing BST, and when does it occur?
recall_questions.answer: O(n) time complexity, which occurs when keys are inserted in sorted or reverse-sorted order, creating a linear spindly tree.

recall_questions.q: Where does a new key land during a standard BST insertion?
recall_questions.answer: It always lands as a new leaf node at the first null child slot reached along the search path.

oa_questions.question: Search in a Binary Search Tree: Given the root of a BST and a target integer val, return the node with that value.
oa_questions.answer: Compare target with current node value. If target < node.val recurse left; if target > node.val recurse right; if equal return node.
oa_questions.approach: BST search path using ordering invariant.

oa_questions.question: Insert into a Binary Search Tree: Insert a value into a BST and return the root.
oa_questions.answer: Traverse to the correct null child slot, instantiate a new TreeNode(val), attach it to the parent, and return root.
oa_questions.approach: Recursive or iterative BST search down to a null child reference.

interesting_facts: Even though simple BSTs can degrade to O(n), randomly built BSTs (inserting keys in random permutation) have an expected height of ~2.99 log2(n), making them balanced on average!
